practicals.label: Activity 1.08
practicals.bookText:
Computing Systems Around Us
**Activity Tasks Detail:** Start with an introduction on computing systems. Students will then research and list various computing systems they use daily, completing a worksheet. In a group sharing session, students will discuss their findings. The class will engage in a discussion to highlight key points, and students will begin preparing a short presentation on a computing system for the next class.
**Output:** Completed worksheets, group insights, and a short presentation on a chosen computing system.
Tidbits
**Internet Systems**
1. When you send an email or browse the internet, data travels through cables and airwaves across the world in just seconds. It's like sending a letter that gets delivered instantly, regardless of distance!
2. The internet is one of the largest man-made systems ever created. It's a vast network of interconnected computers that communicate with each other to share information, much like how our brain's neurons communicate. When you send a message, it travels through multiple networks before reaching its destination, all within seconds.
3. Data on the internet travels at nearly the speed of light! When you send a message or browse a website, your data can cross continents almost instantaneously.
4. There are over 1.5 billion websites on the internet today, and more than 4 billion people are connected to the internet globally. That's more than half of the world's population!
SUMMARY
- A system is a collection of parts that work together to achieve a common goal.
- A system is described by its objective, components, communication among components and environment in which it works.
- Components are the building blocks of any system. Each component plays a specific role and contributes to the overall functionality of the system.
- The environment of a system includes everything external to the system that interacts with it. It consists of all external factors that affect system's operation.
- Systems can be broadly categorized into two types, namely natural and artificial systems.
- Natural systems are those that exist in nature and operate independently of human involvement.
- Artificial systems are designed and constructed by humans.
- Social systems are organized structures created by humans to manage social relationships, governance, and community activities.
- Computer science is the study of how computers work. It looks at what computers can do and what limitations they have.
- A computer is a complex system designed to process data and perform tasks according to a set of instructions.
- The Von Neumann architecture involves several key steps for a CPU to execute instructions, including fetching, decoding, executing, and storing.
- System software is the basic software that helps a computer run and manage its hardware and software resources.
- Application software is the software designed to help users perform specific tasks or activities.
practicals.title: Computing Systems Around Us
practicals.aim: To identify computing systems used in daily life, record how their components work together, share findings, and begin a short presentation on one system.

notes.title: Understanding Systems
notes.answer: A system is an organized set of related components that work together to achieve an objective in an environment.
notes.explanation: A system is a group of related parts that work together in an environment to achieve a purpose. Its objective tells us what it is meant to do; its components do the work, and communication helps them cooperate.
notes.simple: A system is a team of connected parts working together for a purpose.
examples: A car has parts such as an engine, wheels and brakes. Each part has a task, and together they help the car move.
A computer system processes data to provide useful information to users.
steps: Identify the system's objective: what does it aim to do?
Name its components and the role of each one.
Explain how the components communicate or interact.
Identify the environment: what outside factors interact with the system?
notes.checkQuestion: What are the basic features used to describe a system?
notes.checkAnswer: A system has objectives, components, communication among components, and an environment. Its components communicate to achieve its objective.

notes.title: Natural and artificial systems
notes.answer: Natural systems occur in nature; artificial systems are created by people for particular functions or purposes.
notes.explanation: Natural systems exist in nature and operate without human involvement. Artificial systems are made by people for particular functions or purposes. To identify a system, ask whether it occurs naturally or has been created by people.
notes.simple: Natural means found in nature; artificial means made by people.
steps: Ask whether the system exists in nature without people making it.
If it does, classify it as a natural system.
If people created it for a function or purpose, classify it as an artificial system.
notes.checkQuestion: Is a galaxy a natural system or an artificial system?
notes.checkAnswer: A galaxy is a natural system because it occurs in nature. A screw gauge is an artificial system because people make it.

notes.title: System and Science
notes.answer: Natural science describes existing natural systems; design science creates artifacts to achieve specific goals.
notes.explanation: Science helps us understand systems and, in some cases, create new ones. Natural science describes existing natural systems. Design science creates artifacts to achieve goals. Computer science uses methods from both.
notes.simple: Natural science studies what already exists. Design science makes something new to solve a problem.
examples: Studying how species interact in a forest is natural science.
Creating software to manage forest data is design science.
steps: Identify whether the work studies an existing system or creates a new one.
If it studies and describes a natural system, it is natural science.
If it designs an artifact to achieve a goal, it is design science.
Computer science uses methods of both natural science and design science.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of science creates tools or systems to achieve a goal?
notes.checkAnswer: Design science.

notes.title: Computer as a System
notes.answer: A computer is a complex system designed to process data and perform tasks according to a set of instructions.
notes.explanation: A computer works as a system: its components work together to process data and perform tasks. Input devices let users give commands, processing components handle data, storage keeps data, and output devices present results. The motherboard and system bus help components communicate.
notes.simple: A computer system is a team of parts. Each part has a job, and the parts communicate to get work done.
examples: Clicking a document with a mouse gives the computer input; the operating system determines what action to take, and the computer displays the file.
A printer is a peripheral that can produce output from a computer.
steps: A user gives input using a device such as a mouse or keyboard.
The input device sends a signal to the computer.
The operating system receives information from interface components and determines what action to take.
The CPU performs computations and executes commands; data and instructions may be held in RAM or permanent storage.
An output device, such as a monitor, presents the result.
notes.checkQuestion: What carries data between the CPU and other interconnected components?
notes.checkAnswer: The system bus carries data between the CPU and other connected components.

notes.title: How a Von Neumann Computer Works
notes.answer: The Von Neumann architecture has memory, a CPU, input devices, and output devices. Instructions and data share the same memory.
notes.explanation: The Von Neumann architecture uses one memory space for both instructions and data. The CPU fetches an instruction, decodes it, executes it, and stores or sends out the result.
notes.simple: Think of the computer as following a recipe: it gets instructions from memory, understands them, does the work, and saves or displays the result.
examples: A keyboard is an input device; a monitor is an output device.
The data bus transports data between computer components.
steps: Fetch the next instruction from memory.
Decode the instruction to determine what it requires.
Execute it using the ALU and/or Control Unit.
Store the result in memory or send it to an output device.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the four steps in the Von Neumann instruction cycle?
notes.checkAnswer: Fetching, decoding, execution, and storing.

notes.title: Computing Systems
notes.answer: A computing system uses hardware, software, and electricity to process data and perform tasks.
notes.explanation: A computing system needs hardware, software, and electricity to work. Networks and the Internet are also computing systems that connect devices and help them share information.
notes.simple: Hardware is the equipment, software gives it instructions, and electricity powers it. Networks connect devices so they can communicate and share resources.
examples: A school LAN connects computers and printers within the school.
The Internet connects networks across the world.
steps: Identify the hardware: the physical devices.
Identify the software: the instructions and programs.
Check that electricity is available to power the hardware.
For a network, identify how devices connect and share information.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of network connects computers in a specific area, such as a school?
notes.checkAnswer: A LAN connects computers in a specific area, such as one building or school.

notes.title: Understanding systems and computers
notes.answer: A system works through connected components to achieve an objective.
notes.explanation: A system is a group of connected parts that work together to achieve a common objective. Its components interact with one another and with the environment.
notes.simple: A system is a team of parts working together to do a job.
examples: A thermostat takes a temperature input, processes it, and switches a heating or cooling device to help maintain a set temperature.
A computer takes input, processes data, and produces output.
steps: Identify the system's objective: what it is meant to do.
Identify its components and the environment in which it operates.
Explain how the components communicate and work together.
For a computer, trace input, processing, memory or storage, and output.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the main purpose of a system?
notes.checkAnswer: A system is a group of connected components that work together to achieve a common objective.

notes.title: Numbering Systems: Bases and Conversion
notes.answer: The number systems in this section are decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8), and hexadecimal (base 16).
notes.explanation: A number system uses a base to decide its place values and which digits are allowed. To convert from decimal, divide by the new base and read the remainders from bottom to top. To convert a binary number to decimal, add the place values of its 1s.
notes.simple: A base tells you how many different digit values a number system uses. For example, binary uses only 0 and 1, while octal uses 0 through 7.
steps: Identify the base you are converting from and the base you are converting to.
For decimal to binary, octal or hexadecimal, divide repeatedly by 2, 8 or 16, respectively.
Write down each remainder and continue until the quotient is 0.
Read the remainders from bottom to top.
For binary to decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add the results.
notes.checkQuestion: Convert 1010₂ to decimal.

notes.title: Storing whole numbers and integers
notes.answer: The range is 0 to 65,535.
notes.explanation: An unsigned 2-byte whole number uses 16 bits. Its values range from 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1, which is 65,535.
notes.simple: More bits let a computer store a wider range of whole-number values. Signed integers can be negative; unsigned whole numbers cannot.
examples: An unsigned 1-byte whole number ranges from 0 to 255.
An 8-bit signed integer ranges from −128 to 127.
steps: A byte has 8 bits, so 2 bytes have 16 bits.
For an unsigned number, the minimum value is 0.
Find the maximum using 2ⁿ − 1: 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the range of values for an unsigned 2-byte integer?

notes.title: Storing Real Values in Computer Memory
notes.answer: A floating-point value is represented using a sign bit, an exponent, and a mantissa.
notes.explanation: A real number with a fractional part can be written in binary and stored using a sign bit, an exponent, and a mantissa. To convert a decimal fraction to binary, repeatedly multiply it by 2 and record each integer part.
notes.simple: Computers store decimal numbers with fractions by expressing them in binary and dividing their storage into parts.
examples: 5.75 is represented as 1.4375 × 2².
steps: Separate the number into its integer and fractional parts.
To convert a fractional part to binary, multiply it by 2.
Record the integer part of each result, from top to bottom.
Continue with each new fractional part until it reaches zero or the required precision is achieved.
For single precision, use 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 mantissa bits.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the three main components used to represent a floating-point value?
notes.checkAnswer: The sign bit, exponent, and mantissa.

notes.title: Binary Arithmetic Operations
notes.answer: Binary addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are performed using the digits 0 and 1 and the rules for each operation.
notes.explanation: Binary arithmetic uses the digits 0 and 1. Addition uses carries; subtraction can be done by adding the subtrahend's two's complement; multiplication and division follow familiar decimal methods using binary digits.
notes.simple: Work with just 0 and 1. For subtraction, change the subtrahend to its two's complement, add it, and discard the final carry.
steps: For addition, add the bits from right to left and carry 1 when needed.
For subtraction, invert the subtrahend's bits and add 1.
Add the minuend and the two's complement.
Discard the carry bit if one appears.
For multiplication and division, use the familiar long-operation steps with binary digits.
notes.checkQuestion: Add 101₂ and 110₂.

notes.title: Common Text Encoding Schemes
notes.answer: ASCII represents characters using code numbers from 0 to 127. Unicode maps graphic characters used in the world's writing systems and can be encoded in forms such as UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32.
notes.explanation: ASCII assigns a number to each character. Unicode can represent characters from many writing systems, and UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are ways of encoding Unicode characters.
notes.simple: Encoding gives characters a computer-readable form, such as a number or a sequence of bits.
steps: Identify the character.
Look up its code or Unicode code point.
Use the encoding scheme to represent it in binary.
State how many bits or bytes the encoding uses, when required.
notes.checkQuestion: How many bits does standard ASCII use?
notes.checkAnswer: ASCII uses 7 bits and can represent 128 characters.

notes.title: How computers store images, audio, and video
notes.answer: Images use pixels and RGB colour values; audio uses sampling and quantization; videos use frames. Computers store all of them as binary data.
notes.explanation: Images are made from pixels. Each pixel has a colour, represented in a colour image by Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) values. Computers store image, audio, and video files as binary data: sequences of 0s and 1s.
notes.simple: A digital picture is made from tiny coloured dots. A computer stores the information about those dots using 0s and 1s.
examples: A pixel with RGB values (255, 0, 0) is bright red.
A video frame rate tells how many frames are shown each second.
steps: Identify whether the file is an image, audio, or video.
For an image, think of pixels and their RGB colour values.
For audio, remember sampling and quantization.
For video, remember that frames are shown in sequence and measured in frames per second.
Remember that all these files are stored as binary data.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the tiny dots that make up a digital image called?
notes.checkAnswer: A pixel.

notes.title: How computers represent information
notes.explanation: This unit covers how computers represent text, integers, floating-point numbers, and images. It also practises binary arithmetic and signed 4-bit calculations.
notes.simple: A computer stores information as bits: 0s and 1s. Different rules let those bits represent letters, numbers, and pictures.
examples: Unsigned 2-byte integers use 16 bits, so their range is 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1, or 0 to 65,535.
In 4-bit two's complement, −5 is made by writing 5 as 0101, inverting the bits to 1010, then adding 1 to get 1011.
steps: For an unsigned integer with n bits, use the range 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
For a signed 4-bit value, use two's complement: invert the positive number's bits and add 1 to represent its negative.
For binary addition and subtraction, line up the bits and work from right to left, carrying or borrowing as needed.
Unicode assigns code points to characters from many languages.
An image is made of pixels, and RGB represents colour using red, green, and blue.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the range of an unsigned 2-byte integer?
notes.checkAnswer: The range is 0 to 65,535.

notes.title: Analog and Digital Signals
notes.answer: An ADC converts analog signals into digital signals.
notes.explanation: An analog signal changes smoothly and can take any value in a range. A digital signal has only two possible values, 0 and 1. An ADC changes an analog signal into digital form; a DAC changes digital data back into an analog signal.
notes.simple: Analog is smooth and can have many values. Digital uses just 0 and 1. ADC changes analog to digital; DAC changes digital to analog.
examples: A voice entering a microphone is an analog signal; an ADC converts it into digital data.
A DAC converts digital data into an analog signal that a speaker turns into sound.
steps: A microphone captures sound waves, which are analog signals.
An ADC converts the analog signal into digital data made of 0s and 1s.
The digital data can be processed, stored, or transmitted.
A DAC changes the digital data back into an analog signal.
A speaker turns the analog signal into sound waves.
notes.checkQuestion: Which converter changes an analog signal into a digital signal?
notes.checkAnswer: An ADC converts analog signals into digital signals.

notes.title: Boolean functions and basic logic
notes.answer: A Boolean function uses binary inputs and logic operations to produce a binary output.
notes.explanation: A Boolean function takes one or more binary inputs and gives one binary output. Its inputs and output are only 0 or 1. AND, OR and NOT are used to build Boolean functions.
notes.simple: A Boolean function is a rule that takes in 0s and 1s and gives back a 0 or 1.
examples: For F(A, B) = A · B, the output is 1 only when A = 1 and B = 1.
For P = ¬A, if A = 1 then P = 0.
steps: Write the input values: A = 0 and B = 1.
For AND, the output is 1 only if both inputs are 1, so A · B = 0.
For OR, the output is 1 if at least one input is 1, so A + B = 1.
notes.checkQuestion: If A = 0 and B = 1, what are A · B and A + B?
notes.checkAnswer: For A = 1 and B = 0, A · B = 0 and A + B = 1.

notes.title: Simplifying Boolean Functions
notes.answer: A
notes.explanation: Boolean simplification uses algebra rules to make a function shorter while keeping the same output. For example, A + A·B = A by the absorption law. Another example is A + A̅·B = A + B, using the distributive, complement and identity laws.
notes.simple: Use Boolean rules to remove unnecessary parts of an expression without changing its value.
steps: Look for a pair or pattern that matches a Boolean law.
Apply one law at a time and show its name if required.
Continue until no part can be simplified further.
notes.checkQuestion: Simplify A + A·B.
notes.checkAnswer: A

notes.title: Digital systems and Boolean logic
notes.answer: A half-adder produces its carry using the AND operation: Carry = A · B.
notes.explanation: Boolean algebra works with two values, 0 and 1. It describes how logic gates combine binary inputs to produce binary outputs.
notes.simple: Think of Boolean algebra as rules for working with switches that are either off (0) or on (1).
examples: If F = A + B, then F is 1 whenever at least one input is 1.
For a half-adder, Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B.
steps: Write down the possible binary input combinations.
Apply the Boolean expression to each input combination.
Use the resulting outputs to describe or build the logic circuit.
notes.checkQuestion: Which operation produces a carry in a half-adder?
notes.checkAnswer: A · B

notes.title: Troubleshooting systems step by step
notes.answer: Troubleshooting helps identify and fix system problems quickly so systems can operate smoothly and efficiently.
notes.explanation: Troubleshooting means finding out what is wrong with a system and following steps to fix it. Work through the steps in order, then check that the system works and record what you did.
notes.simple: Be a tech detective: notice the problem, work out what might cause it, test your idea, fix it, check the result, and write down what happened.
examples: If a laptop will not turn on, possible causes include a dead battery, a faulty power cord, or an internal hardware issue.
If a printer is not working properly, a paper jam may be the cause; clearing it may fix the problem.
steps: Identify Problem
Establish a Theory of Probable Cause
Test the Theory to Determine the Cause
Establish a Plan of Action to Resolve the Problem
Implement the Solution
Verify Full System Functionality
Document Findings, Actions, and Outcomes
notes.checkQuestion: What is the first step in the systematic process of troubleshooting?
notes.checkAnswer: Identify the problem.

notes.title: A careful way to troubleshoot
notes.answer: Troubleshooting is a systematic way to identify and resolve problems, then check and record the results.
notes.explanation: Troubleshooting means finding what is wrong, checking possible causes, fixing the issue, and confirming that the system works again. Work carefully and record what you did.
notes.simple: Find the problem, check its cause, fix it, and make sure the computer works properly.
examples: If an application freezes, open Task Manager with Ctrl + Alt + Delete, select the unresponsive application, and click “End Task.”
If a computer is overheating, improve its airflow and clean dust from its vents and fans.
steps: Identify and define the problem.
Establish a theory of probable cause.
Test the theory.
Establish a plan of action.
Implement the solution.
Verify full system functionality.
Document findings, actions, and outcomes.
notes.checkQuestion: What should you do after implementing a solution?
notes.checkAnswer: Identify the problem first, then decide what may be causing it and test that idea.

notes.title: A systematic way to solve system problems
notes.answer: Identify the problem.
notes.explanation: Troubleshooting is a systematic way to identify and resolve problems in a system. Follow the steps in order: identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, plan and implement a solution, verify the system, and document what happened.
notes.simple: Troubleshooting means finding out what is wrong, fixing it carefully, and checking that the system works afterward.
examples: If a laptop will not turn on, first note the problem, then consider whether the battery or power supply may be faulty.
If a printer will not print, check its power, connection, paper, and ink or toner before deciding on a solution.
steps: Identify and clearly describe the problem.
Establish a theory of probable cause.
Test the theory to determine the cause.
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem.
Implement the solution.
Verify full system functionality.
Document findings, actions, and outcomes.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the first step in the systematic troubleshooting process?
notes.checkAnswer: Identify the problem.

notes.title: System software and application software
notes.answer: System software manages system resources and provides a platform for applications; application software helps users perform specific tasks.
notes.explanation: Software is a collection of programs and instructions that tell a computer what to do and how to do. System software is designed to manage the system resources and provide a platform for application software to run. For example, Windows is system software, while Microsoft Word is application software.
notes.simple: System software helps run the computer. Application software helps you do a particular task.
examples: Windows manages computer resources; Microsoft Word helps a user create documents.
steps: Identify what the software is mainly for.
If it manages system resources or supports applications, classify it as system software.
If it helps a user perform a specific task, classify it as application software.
Use examples to check: Windows is system software; Microsoft Word is application software.
notes.checkQuestion: Is Microsoft Word system software or application software?
notes.checkAnswer: Application software.

notes.title: Introduction to System Software
notes.answer: System software manages computer resources, supports applications and helps hardware devices work with the operating system.
notes.explanation: System software helps the computer and its hardware work properly and provides a platform for applications. Its main parts in this section are operating systems, utility programs and device drivers.
notes.simple: System software is the computer's helper software: it manages the computer, keeps it working well and helps it communicate with devices.
examples: Windows is an operating system that manages computer resources and provides a user interface.
A printer driver translates computer instructions into instructions the printer can understand.
steps: An operating system manages the computer's hardware and software.
It manages resources such as the CPU, memory, disk drives and peripheral devices.
It provides a user interface, such as a GUI or CLI, and runs applications.
Utility programs help maintain the computer, protect it or manage files.
Device drivers translate instructions so that the operating system and hardware devices can communicate.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a device driver help the computer and a hardware device do?
notes.checkAnswer: A device driver helps the operating system and a hardware device communicate.

notes.title: Application Software
notes.answer: Application software refers to programs designed to perform specific tasks for users, ranging from productivity and creativity to entertainment and education.
notes.explanation: Application software helps people do particular tasks. The type of application depends on the task: word processors work with documents, spreadsheets work with data, and graphic design programs work with visual content.
notes.simple: Application software is a program that helps you do a particular job, such as writing, working with data, or making designs.
examples: Microsoft Word is used to create and edit documents.
Microsoft Excel is used to organize data and make calculations or charts.
Adobe Illustrator is used to create logos and scalable graphics.
steps: Identify the task: documents, data, or visual content.
Choose the matching type of application software.
Name a suitable example, such as Word, Excel, or Photoshop.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one main purpose of spreadsheet software?
notes.checkAnswer: It organizes, analyzes, and stores data in tabular form.

notes.title: Understanding Software Systems
notes.answer: System software manages and supports a computer system; application software performs specific tasks for users.
notes.explanation: System software runs and supports the computer, while application software helps users complete particular tasks. An operating system manages the computer's resources and provides an interface. Utilities maintain the system, and device drivers help the operating system communicate with hardware. Applications include word processors, spreadsheets, presentation programs, and graphic design software.
notes.simple: System software helps the computer work. Application software helps the user do a task.
examples: Windows is an operating system; Disk Cleanup is utility software.
Microsoft Word is application software used to create and edit text documents.
steps: Identify whether the software supports the computer or performs a task for the user.
Name system software examples such as operating systems, utilities, and device drivers.
Name application software examples such as word processors and spreadsheets.
For maintenance, use utilities to check, clean, protect, or back up the system.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of software is used to enhance system performance and security?
notes.checkAnswer: Utility software

notes.title: Network as a System
notes.answer: A computer network is a system of linked devices and computers that may exchange data and operate together.
notes.explanation: A computer network links devices so they can exchange data and work together. Nodes are the connected devices, and links connect those nodes. Switches forward data within a network; routers connect different networks. Networks help people share resources, communicate, and collaborate.
notes.simple: A network is a group of connected devices that can share information and resources.
examples: Several office computers share one printer.
Employees at different locations meet through video conferencing.
steps: Identify the nodes: these are devices connected to the network.
Identify the links: these connect the nodes, either by wire or wirelessly.
Use switches to forward data within a network.
Use routers to connect different networks and direct data packets.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a switch do in a network?
notes.checkAnswer: A switch forwards data between nodes within a network.

notes.title: The five components of data communication
notes.answer: The five components are sender, receiver, message, protocol, and medium.
notes.explanation: Data communication is the exchange of data between a sender and a receiver through a medium. The five components tell us who sends the data, who receives it, what is sent, which rules are followed, and how the data travels.
notes.simple: Data communication means sending data from one device to another. Remember the five parts: sender, receiver, message, protocol, and medium.
examples: A computer sends an email: the computer is the sender, the smartphone is the receiver, and the email content is the message.
The data may travel through an Ethernet cable or Wi-Fi; these are examples of a medium.
steps: Identify the device that sends the data: the sender.
Identify the device that receives the data: the receiver.
Identify the data being sent: the message.
Identify the rules for communicating: the protocol.
Identify the path the data travels through: the medium.
notes.checkQuestion: Which component is the set of rules governing data communication?
notes.checkAnswer: Protocol.

notes.title: Networking Devices
notes.answer: Switches connect and direct data between devices within a network; routers direct packets between networks; access points connect wireless devices to a wired network.
notes.explanation: A switch connects devices within a network and uses MAC addresses to send data to the intended device. A router connects different networks and directs data packets between them. An access point connects wireless devices to a wired network.
notes.simple: A switch directs data inside a network, a router directs data between networks, and an access point links wireless devices to a wired network.
examples: A switch sends a packet to the computer whose MAC address matches the packet’s destination address.
A router directs packets between a home network and another network.
steps: Identify whether the data is moving within one network or between networks.
For devices communicating within a network, a switch uses destination MAC addresses to forward data.
For data moving between networks, a router finds a path and directs the packets.
For wireless devices joining a wired network, an access point receives and transmits data wirelessly.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a router do with data packets?
notes.checkAnswer: A router directs data packets between different networks.

notes.title: Network Topologies
notes.answer: A network topology is the arrangement of devices in a network.
notes.explanation: A network topology describes how devices (nodes) are arranged and connected. The main types in this section are bus, star, ring, and mesh.
notes.simple: Topology is the shape or pattern of the connections between devices in a network.
examples: In a star topology, a central switch or hub connects to the other devices.
In a mesh topology, every device connects to every other device.
steps: Identify how the devices are connected.
Match that arrangement to bus, star, ring, or mesh.
Remember the important feature or weakness of that topology.
notes.checkQuestion: Which topology connects each device to every other device?
notes.checkAnswer: Mesh topology.

notes.title: Choosing a Transmission Mode
notes.answer: Simplex sends in one direction only; Half-Duplex allows both directions one at a time; Full-Duplex allows both directions simultaneously.
notes.explanation: Transmission modes describe the direction and timing of data flow between devices. Simplex is one-way, Half-Duplex is two-way but takes turns, and Full-Duplex is two-way at the same time.
notes.simple: Ask two questions: Can data go both ways? Can it go both ways at the same time?
steps: Check whether data travels in one direction or both directions.
If it travels in one direction only, the mode is Simplex.
If it travels in both directions but the devices take turns, the mode is Half-Duplex.
If both devices can send and receive at the same time, the mode is Full-Duplex.
notes.checkQuestion: Two people use walkie-talkies and take turns speaking. Which transmission mode is this?
notes.checkAnswer: Half-Duplex

notes.title: What does the Network Layer do?
notes.answer: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and determines the best path for data to travel from source to destination.
notes.explanation: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and selects a path from source to destination. For example, it is like a GPS choosing a route from home to school. The Data Link Layer handles node-to-node transfer, while the Network Layer handles transfer between networks.
notes.simple: The Network Layer is like a GPS for data: it helps data travel between networks by choosing a path.
examples: A GPS finding a route is an example of the Network Layer choosing a path.
IP addresses help the Network Layer route data between networks.
steps: Identify the source and destination networks.
Use IP addresses to route the data.
Determine the best path from source to destination.
notes.checkQuestion: Which OSI layer determines the best path for data to travel between networks?
notes.checkAnswer: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and determines the best path from source to destination.

notes.title: IPv4 and IPv6 address sizes
notes.answer: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits.
notes.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits, so it has 2³² = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses. IPv6 uses 128 bits and was designed to provide many more addresses as the number of internet-connected devices grew. The textbook’s IPv4 example, 172.16.254.1, has four decimal parts, each corresponding to an 8-bit binary group.
notes.simple: IPv4 is like a set of 4.3 billion address labels. IPv6 uses far more bits, so it can provide vastly more labels for connected devices.
examples: IPv4: 172.16.254.1 has four 8-bit groups.
IPv6: 2001:0000:130F:0000:0000:0900:876A:130B is an example of an IPv6 address.
steps: Count the bits in an IPv4 address: 32.
Calculate its possible addresses: 2³² = 4,294,967,296.
An IPv4 address is written as four decimal numbers, each from 0 to 255.
Count the bits in an IPv6 address: 128.
Remember that IPv6 was designed to address the depletion of IPv4 addresses.
notes.checkQuestion: How many bits does an IPv6 address use?
notes.checkAnswer: IPv6 uses a 128-bit address scheme.

notes.title: Protocols, DNS and DHCP
notes.answer: Protocols are sets of rules that govern data communication. DNS translates domain names to IP addresses, and DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network.
notes.explanation: Protocols are rules for communication between devices. DNS looks up the IP address for a domain name, while DHCP automatically gives an IP address to a device on a network.
notes.simple: DNS finds the address of a website. DHCP gives a connected device its network address.
examples: Typing www.example.com in a browser: DNS translates the domain name to its IP address.
Connecting a device to Wi-Fi: DHCP assigns the device an IP address.
steps: Identify what the device or user needs.
Use DNS to translate a domain name to an IP address.
Use DHCP to assign an IP address automatically when a device connects to a network.
notes.checkQuestion: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network?
notes.checkAnswer: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network.

notes.title: Network Security
notes.answer: Network security uses measures such as firewalls, encryption, and authentication to protect data and prevent unauthorized access to networks.
notes.explanation: Network security protects data and networks from unauthorized access and attacks. Firewalls monitor and control network traffic, encryption makes data unreadable without the correct decryption key, and passwords and authentication help ensure that only authorized users can access network resources.
notes.simple: Network security is like protecting a house: a firewall is the gatekeeper, encryption is a secret code, and a password helps check who is allowed in.
examples: A firewall can block unwanted network traffic.
A shift cipher changes “Hello” to “Khoor” by moving each letter three places down the alphabet.
steps: Use a firewall to monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic.
Encrypt sensitive data so that only someone with the correct decryption key can understand it.
Use passwords and authentication to check that users are authorized.
Watch for threats such as malware, phishing, DoS attacks, and man-in-the-middle attacks.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a firewall do?
notes.checkAnswer: A firewall monitors and controls network traffic according to security rules.

notes.title: Choosing a network type by its coverage
notes.answer: A CAN connects multiple LANs within a limited geographical area, such as a university campus.
notes.explanation: Choose the network type by looking at the size and area it covers. A few personal devices nearby use a PAN; devices in one home, school, or office use a LAN; multiple LANs across a campus use a CAN or across a city use a MAN; a very large geographical area uses a WAN.
notes.simple: Think about how far the network reaches: personal devices, one local place, a campus, a city, or a very large area.
examples: A smartphone connected to a wireless headset by Bluetooth forms a PAN.
A network connecting different branch offices of a company across countries is a WAN.
steps: Identify the area covered by the network.
Check whether it connects personal devices, one limited area, a campus, a city, or a large geographical area.
Match that area to PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, or WAN.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of network connects several LANs within a university campus?
notes.checkAnswer: CAN (Campus Area Network).

notes.title: Real-World Applications of Computer Networks
notes.answer: Businesses use intranets to share information and resources securely; educational institutions use networks for online learning and educational resources; healthcare networks support sharing patient information, telemedicine, and access to medical databases.
notes.explanation: Computer networks are useful in business, education, and healthcare. They help people communicate, share resources, and manage information.
notes.simple: Networks connect people and information. Businesses use them to work together, schools use them for learning, and hospitals use them to manage patient information.
examples: Companies use intranets to share information and resources securely within the organization.
Hospitals use Electronic Health Records (EHR) systems to store and retrieve patient data efficiently.
steps: Identify the setting: business, education, or healthcare.
State what the network helps people do in that setting.
Give a relevant example, such as an intranet, LMS, or EHR system.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one network application in each of business, education, and healthcare.
notes.checkAnswer: Networks are used in business to communicate and share resources, in education to provide online learning and educational resources, and in healthcare to share patient information and access medical databases.

notes.title: Standard Protocols in TCP/IP Communications
notes.answer: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses; DNS translates domain names to IP addresses.
notes.explanation: TCP/IP is the main suite of protocols used for internet communication. TCP provides reliable data transfer, while IP handles addressing and routing. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses, and DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses.
notes.simple: Think of these protocols as different helpers: TCP checks that data transfers reliably, IP handles packet addresses and routes, DNS looks up IP addresses from domain names, and DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically.
examples: When a device needs an IP address automatically, DHCP performs that task.
When a domain name needs to be translated into an IP address, DNS performs that task.
steps: Identify the task: reliable transfer, addressing and routing, faster transfer, name translation, or automatic IP assignment.
Match the task to the protocol: TCP, IP, UDP, DNS, or DHCP, respectively.
notes.checkQuestion: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses, and which protocol translates domain names to IP addresses?
notes.checkAnswer: TCP provides reliable data transfer; UDP provides faster, but less reliable, data transfer.

notes.title: Network security methods
notes.answer: Firewalls, encryption, and antivirus software work together to provide robust network security.
notes.explanation: Network security protects data and helps prevent unauthorized access. Your textbook describes three methods: firewalls monitor and control network traffic, encryption converts data into a secure format, and antivirus software detects and removes malicious software.
notes.simple: A firewall checks network traffic, encryption scrambles data into a secure format, and antivirus software finds and removes harmful software.
steps: Firewall: Monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic.
Encryption: Protects data by converting it into a secure format.
Antivirus software: Detects and removes malicious software.
Example: A combination of firewalls, encryption, and antivirus software provides robust network security.
notes.checkQuestion: What does encryption do to data?
notes.checkAnswer: Encryption converts data into a secure format.

notes.title: Computer Networks: Unit Review
notes.answer: A computer network connects devices for data communication and resource sharing.
notes.explanation: A computer network connects devices so they can communicate and share resources. Data travels according to protocols; devices such as routers and switches help move it, while security tools help protect it.
notes.simple: A network is a group of connected devices that can exchange data and share things such as files or printers.
examples: A school network can let many computers use one printer.
DNS finds the IP address linked to a website name.
steps: Connect devices using a suitable network medium and devices.
Use protocols to organise and deliver data.
Use network services such as DNS and DHCP where needed.
Protect the network with tools such as firewalls and encryption.
notes.checkQuestion: Which device directs data packets between different networks?
notes.checkAnswer: A router directs data packets between networks.

notes.title: Computational Thinking: Four Useful Tools
notes.answer: Computational thinking is a problem-solving process that uses skills such as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithms.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking is a way to work through complex problems so that the solution can be carried out by a computer. Its four key components are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithms.
notes.simple: Think of computational thinking as a problem-solving toolkit: split a big task into parts, notice patterns, ignore details that do not matter, and follow clear steps.
examples: To build a birdhouse, split the task into designing it, gathering materials, cutting the wood, assembling the pieces, decorating it, and installing it.
The areas of squares with sides 1, 2, and 3 are 1, 4, and 9. These are also the sums 1, 1 + 3, and 1 + 3 + 5.
steps: Understand the problem and what needs to be done.
Use decomposition to divide a complex task into smaller tasks.
Use pattern recognition to spot similarities or regularities.
Use abstraction to focus on necessary details and leave out unnecessary ones.
Write an algorithm: a precise sequence of instructions to reach the goal.
notes.checkQuestion: What is decomposition?
notes.checkAnswer: Decomposition means breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts.

notes.title: Principles of Computational Thinking
notes.answer: The three principles in this section are problem understanding, problem simplification, and solution selection and design.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking starts by understanding the problem, then simplifying it into manageable parts, and choosing and planning a suitable solution.
notes.simple: First understand what needs to be done. Then divide the work into smaller parts and plan a suitable way to complete them.
examples: Before building a school website, find out what pages it needs, who will use it, and what tools are available.
To design a website, split the work into layout, content, and functionality.
steps: Understand the problem and identify its requirements.
Set clear objectives for the outcome.
Break a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
Evaluate possible approaches and select an efficient solution.
Create a detailed plan or algorithm for the solution.
notes.checkQuestion: What does problem simplification mean?
notes.checkAnswer: Break the problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.

notes.title: Choosing an Algorithm Design Method
notes.answer: Flowcharts and pseudocode are two ways to describe an algorithm. Flowcharts use graphical symbols and arrows. Pseudocode uses plain language and a structured format.
notes.explanation: Flowcharts show an algorithm with symbols and arrows; pseudocode describes its steps in simple, structured language. Use the method that makes the algorithm easiest to understand and check.
notes.simple: A flowchart is a picture of the steps. Pseudocode is a written plan of the steps.
examples: A flowchart uses a diamond for a decision such as “Is the item available?”
Pseudocode can use if/else to print “Even” or “Odd”.
steps: Identify the steps and decisions needed to solve the problem.
Use a flowchart when you want to show the overall flow visually.
Use pseudocode when you want to describe the logic step by step in words.
Check that each decision has the correct branches and that the process can reach an end.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one main difference between a flowchart and pseudocode?
notes.checkAnswer: A flowchart is visual and uses symbols and arrows; pseudocode uses plain language in a structured format.

notes.title: Checking how algorithms work
notes.answer: A dry run checks an algorithm step by step using sample data.
notes.explanation: Time complexity describes how an algorithm’s running time changes as the input gets bigger. Space complexity describes how much memory it uses. Dry runs and simulations help check that an algorithm works as intended.
notes.simple: Time complexity is about time and steps; space complexity is about memory. A dry run is a careful test using sample data.
examples: If you check each name in a list one by one, a longer list may take more steps.
A dry run uses sample data to check an algorithm without actually running a program.
steps: Choose sample input data.
Follow the algorithm one step at a time.
Keep track of the values and actions at each step.
Check whether the result is correct.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a dry run use to check an algorithm?
notes.checkAnswer: A dry run is a manual check of an algorithm using sample data.

notes.title: Dry Run
notes.answer: A dry run involves manually going through the algorithm with sample data to identify any errors.
notes.explanation: A dry run means following an algorithm manually with sample data. You track what happens at each step, including the values of variables and the output. This can help you spot logic errors before using a computer.
notes.simple: A dry run is like acting out an algorithm by hand, one step at a time.
examples: For the addition flowchart, use A = 3 and B = 5: Sum = 3 + 5 = 8.
For FindMax, use num1 = 10 and num2 = 15: 10 > 15 is False, so max = 15.
steps: Choose sample data for the algorithm.
Follow each instruction in order.
Check conditions and update variable values when needed.
Record the output and check whether it makes sense.
notes.checkQuestion: If num1 = 4 and num2 = 9, what value does FindMax output?
notes.checkAnswer: If num1 = 4 and num2 = 9, the output max is 9.

notes.title: Practising algorithms with LARP
notes.answer: LARP stands for Logic of Algorithms for resolution of Problems. It lets learners run algorithms and observe their results.
notes.explanation: LARP is a tool for trying out algorithms: you provide inputs, run the instructions, and observe the outputs. It uses simple commands such as START, READ, WRITE, IF...THEN...ELSE, and END.
notes.simple: LARP is like a practice space where you can run an algorithm and see what it does.
examples: An even-or-odd algorithm reads a number and displays whether it is even or odd.
A salary algorithm can calculate annual salary and display whether tax applies.
steps: Start the algorithm with START.
Use READ to get input and WRITE to display messages or results.
Use IF...THEN...ELSE when the algorithm must make a decision.
Finish the algorithm with END.
Run the algorithm with different inputs and check its outputs.
notes.checkQuestion: What does LARP help you do with an algorithm?
notes.checkAnswer: LARP helps you run algorithms and see how different inputs affect their outputs.

notes.title: Error Identification and Debugging
notes.answer: Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in an algorithm or flowchart.
notes.explanation: Algorithms and flowcharts can contain errors, or bugs. Debugging means finding and fixing them. You can trace the steps, use comments, check decision conditions, and test smaller parts separately.
notes.simple: Debugging is checking an algorithm to find what is wrong and then fixing it.
examples: If an algorithm tries to divide by zero while it runs, that is a runtime error.
If a decision uses the wrong condition and gives the wrong result, that is a logical error.
steps: Read any error message carefully.
Trace the algorithm step by step with sample data.
Check that decision conditions are correct.
Use comments to clarify what each part should do.
Break the problem into smaller parts and test them separately.
notes.checkQuestion: An algorithm runs, but gives the wrong answer because a decision condition is incorrect. What type of error is this?
notes.checkAnswer: A logical error.

notes.title: Computational Thinking: Solve Problems Step by Step
notes.answer: Computational thinking is a systematic, logical approach to understanding and solving problems. It uses decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design.
notes.explanation: Computational thinking is a way to solve problems systematically. It includes understanding the problem, breaking it into parts, finding patterns, focusing on important details, and designing and checking a solution.
notes.simple: Computational thinking means working out a problem carefully, in manageable steps, before or while using a computer.
examples: A recipe gives ordered instructions for preparing food, much like an algorithm.
A school timetable can be simplified by focusing on each class's time and room, rather than every detail about the school.
steps: Understand what the problem asks and identify the information you need.
Decompose the problem into smaller parts.
Look for similarities or repeated steps (patterns).
Ignore unnecessary details and focus on what matters (abstraction).
Design a step-by-step algorithm, using pseudocode or a flowchart if helpful.
Dry run the solution with sample data and debug any errors.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one way computational thinking can make a difficult problem easier.
notes.checkAnswer: Break the task into smaller parts, find repeated steps, focus on the important information, and write and test a clear set of instructions.

notes.title: Web Development
notes.answer: Web development is the process of creating websites and web applications using programming languages and tools.
notes.explanation: Web development means using programming languages and tools to create, design, build, and maintain websites and web applications. HTML gives a page its structure, CSS controls its appearance, and JavaScript can make it interactive.
notes.simple: Web development is making and looking after websites. HTML provides structure, CSS makes pages look attractive, and JavaScript adds interactive features.
examples: A student uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to make a personal website; this is web development.
A business creates and maintains a website to sell its products; this is also web development.
steps: Use HTML to create the structure of a web page.
Use CSS to control how the page looks.
Use JavaScript to add interactive features.
Build, test, and maintain the website.
notes.checkQuestion: Which technology makes a web page interactive?
notes.checkAnswer: Web development is the process of creating websites and web applications using programming languages and tools.

notes.title: Basic Components of Web Development
notes.answer: JavaScript.
notes.explanation: A website has a front end that users see, a back end that handles behind-the-scenes work, and full-stack development that includes both. HTML structures page content, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds interactivity. The back end can use web servers, databases, and programming languages such as PHP, Python, and Ruby.
notes.simple: The front end is what users see. The back end does the hidden work. Full-stack development covers both.
examples: A login form is part of the front end; checking login details and accessing user data are back-end tasks.
A full-stack developer can work on both the login screen and the authentication and database interaction behind it.
steps: Identify what the user sees and interacts with: this is the front end.
Use HTML to structure the content, CSS to style it, and JavaScript to make it interactive.
Identify the behind-the-scenes work, such as servers, data, and application logic: this is the back end.
A full-stack developer works on both the front end and the back end.
notes.checkQuestion: Which front-end technology adds interactivity to web pages?
notes.checkAnswer: JavaScript adds interactivity to web pages.

notes.title: Getting Started with HTML
notes.answer: HTML is the standard language used to create web pages.
notes.explanation: HTML is the standard language used to create web pages. You write HTML in a text editor, save the file with the .html extension, and open it in a web browser to see the page.
notes.simple: HTML is the code used to build a web page. Write it in a text editor, save it as a .html file, and view it in a browser.
examples: Save a page as My_first_website.html.
Use a text editor such as Notepad++ to write HTML, then open the saved file in a browser.
steps: Open a text editor.
Write the HTML code.
Save the file with a .html extension.
Open the file in a web browser.
Refresh the browser after changing the file.
notes.checkQuestion: What file extension should you add when saving an HTML file?
notes.checkAnswer: Save the file with the .html extension.

notes.title: The Basic Structure of an HTML Page
notes.answer:
A paired tag has an opening tag and a closing tag, such as

and

.
notes.explanation: A basic HTML document has an outer structure that helps the browser understand the page. The head contains information such as the title, while the body contains the content shown on the page. Tags organise that content.
notes.simple: Think of an HTML page as a container: the head holds page information, and the body holds what people see.
examples: <head><title>My Page</title></head>

Welcome

Hello!
steps: Start with <!DOCTYPE html> to identify the document as HTML5.
Put the page inside the root <html> element.
Use <head> for information such as the title.
Use <body> for the visible page content.

Use tags such as
