for a paragraph.
notes.checkQuestion: Which kind of tag has an opening tag and a closing tag?
notes.checkAnswer:
A paired tag has an opening tag and a closing tag, such as

and

.

notes.title: Creating Content with HTML
notes.answer: HTML content is the information on a web page that users read and interact with, such as text, images, videos, links, and other elements.
notes.explanation:
HTML content is the information people read or interact with on a web page. For example, a paragraph uses `

...

`, and a link uses `link text`.
notes.simple: HTML content is what a web page shows people. Tags tell the browser what kind of content each part is.
examples:
`

Welcome to my page.

`
`Visit Example.com`
steps: Use `<h1>` to `<h6>` for headings, from the main title to less important subheadings.

Put paragraph text between `

` and `

`.
Create a link with `link text`.
Add an image with ``.
Use `<ul>` for a bulleted list or `<ol>` for a numbered list, with each item inside `<li>` tags.
Create a table with `<table>`, rows with `<tr>`, headings with `<th>`, and data cells with `<td>`. Comments go between `<!--` and `-->`.
notes.checkQuestion: Which tags create a numbered list, and what tag wraps each list item?
notes.checkAnswer: Use `<ul>` for a bulleted list and `<ol>` for a numbered list; put each item inside `<li>` tags.

notes.title: Styling webpages with CSS
notes.answer: CSS styles HTML elements using rules made of selectors and declarations.
notes.explanation: CSS styles HTML elements. A CSS rule has a selector that chooses the elements and declarations that tell the browser what styles to apply.
notes.simple: Think of CSS as instructions for how HTML content should look.
examples: h1 { color: red; } changes the text colour of all h1 headings to red.
body { background-color: blue; } gives the page a blue background.
steps: Write a selector for the HTML element you want to style.
Add braces after the selector.
Inside the braces, write each property followed by a colon and its value.
End each declaration with a semicolon.
notes.checkQuestion: In a CSS rule, what does the selector do?
notes.checkAnswer: A selector chooses the HTML elements to style; declarations give the properties and values.

notes.title: Introduction to JavaScript
notes.answer: JavaScript makes web pages interactive by responding to user actions and input.
notes.explanation: JavaScript is a programming language that is used to make websites interactive and engaging. It can respond to actions such as clicks, read information entered in a form, and change page content or styles.
notes.simple: HTML provides the page elements, and JavaScript makes them respond to users.
examples: When a button is clicked, JavaScript can display an alert message.
JavaScript can change a page's background color when a button is clicked.
steps: Put the JavaScript code in a <script> element or link an external JavaScript file.
Write a function to perform the task.
Connect the function to an event, such as onclick.
When the event occurs, the function runs.
notes.checkQuestion: Which HTML event runs when a user clicks an element?
notes.checkAnswer: onclick

notes.title: Developing, Testing, and Debugging Web Pages
notes.answer: The browser console in the developer tools.
notes.explanation: Debugging helps you find and fix problems in code. Testing checks that a web page works correctly across browsers, devices, and for its users.
notes.simple: Debugging is like finding and fixing a mistake. Testing is checking that the page works as expected.
examples: If a link does not open the intended page, check that its URL and file path are correct.
If a page looks different on a phone, use responsive design mode to check it at different screen sizes.
steps: Open the browser developer tools and check the console for errors.
Read the error message carefully to understand the problem.
Check the code line by line for issues such as missing semicolons, unmatched braces, or incorrect variable names.
Check links, HTML tag structure, and CSS selectors when a page does not work or look right.
Test the page in different browsers and on different screen sizes.
Ask users to try the page and give feedback.
notes.checkQuestion: Which browser tool can show error messages and debug output?
notes.checkAnswer: Use the browser console to view error messages and debug output.

notes.title: How HTML, CSS, and JavaScript work together
notes.answer: CSS controls the appearance of a web page.
notes.explanation: HTML provides the structure of a web page, CSS controls its appearance, and JavaScript adds behaviour. They work together to create websites.
notes.simple: Think of a web page as a house: HTML is its structure, CSS is its decoration, and JavaScript makes things happen.
examples:
HTML:

Hello!

creates a paragraph.
CSS: p { color: blue; } makes paragraph text blue.
steps: Use HTML tags to arrange content such as headings, paragraphs, images, and links.
Use CSS rules to style that content.
Use JavaScript to respond to user actions and change page content or appearance.
notes.checkQuestion: Which language controls the appearance of a web page?
notes.checkAnswer: HTML

notes.title: Understanding Data
notes.answer: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.
notes.explanation: Data is raw facts collected about things around us. It can be processed to make useful information. Data may be numbers, words, measurements, observations, images, or sounds, and can come from different sources.
notes.simple: Data is unprocessed information we collect. When we work with it, it can help us understand something or make a decision.
examples: Weather data includes temperature, humidity, and wind speed collected from weather stations.
A store may record the number of products sold and their prices.
steps: Collect facts about something.
Process those facts.
Use them to produce useful information.
notes.checkQuestion: What is data?
notes.checkAnswer: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.

notes.title: Choosing the right data type
notes.answer: Qualitative data is descriptive or categorical; quantitative data is numerical. Nominal categories have no order, ordinal categories have a meaningful order, discrete data is countable, and continuous data can take any value within a range.
notes.explanation: Data types describe what kind of information we have. Qualitative data uses descriptions or categories; quantitative data uses numbers. Qualitative data may be nominal or ordinal, while quantitative data may be discrete or continuous.
notes.simple: Ask what the data tells you: a label or description is qualitative; a measured or counted number is quantitative. Then check whether categories have an order or whether numbers are counted or measured.
examples: A student's favourite fruit is qualitative, nominal data: it is a category with no implied order.
A student's height is quantitative, continuous data: it is measured and can include decimals.
steps: If the information is a label or category, it is qualitative.
If qualitative categories have no order, they are nominal; if they have a meaningful order, they are ordinal.
If the information is a number, it is quantitative.
If a number counts separate items, it is discrete; if it measures a value that can include fractions or decimals, it is continuous.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of data is the number of students in a class, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: The number of students is discrete data because it is counted in separate whole numbers.

notes.title: Organising and Analysing Data
notes.answer: Organised data is easier to find, understand, compare and analyse.
notes.explanation: Organising data makes it clearer, quicker to use and easier to analyse. Data can be collected using methods such as surveys, questionnaires, interviews and observations, then organised into tables, charts or graphs. Information from online sources can be extracted and integrated to build a fuller understanding of a topic.
notes.simple: Put information in a neat, useful form so it is easier to understand and compare.
examples: A table of students' marks makes it easier to compare their scores in different subjects.
For a project on social media, you could collect information from several websites, save relevant statistics and combine similar findings.
steps: Collect information using a suitable method, such as a survey or observation.
Arrange the information neatly in a table, chart or graph.
Look for patterns, trends or similarities.
Combine useful information from different sources when a fuller picture is needed.
notes.checkQuestion: Why can organising data into tables or charts help when analysing it?
notes.checkAnswer: Organising data into tables, charts and graphs makes it clearer and easier to find, compare and analyse.

notes.title: Structured and Unstructured Data
notes.answer: Structured data is organised in a format that is easy to search and analyse; unstructured data is free-form and does not fit a specific format.
notes.explanation: Structured data is organised and formatted to be easily searchable and analysable. Unstructured data is more free-form and doesn't fit into a specific format. Structured data is often stored in rows and columns, while unstructured data includes items such as emails, social media posts, videos, and images.
notes.simple: Structured data is neatly arranged. Unstructured data is not arranged in a fixed format.
examples: A student spreadsheet with columns for Student ID, Name, Class, and Fee Status is structured data.
An email or a video is unstructured data.
steps: Look for a fixed arrangement, such as rows and columns.
If the data is arranged in a searchable format, identify it as structured data.
If it is free-form and does not fit a specific format, identify it as unstructured data.
notes.checkQuestion: Is a spreadsheet of student records structured or unstructured data, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: A student spreadsheet is structured data because it is organised in rows and columns. A video is unstructured data because it does not fit into that format.

notes.title: Choosing a way to store data
notes.answer: The four technologies are spreadsheets, databases, data warehouses, and NoSQL.
notes.explanation: Data storage techniques are ways to save and organise information so it can be accessed and used later. Spreadsheets arrange data in rows and columns; databases store structured data in tables; data warehouses store and analyse large amounts of data from different sources; NoSQL databases can store flexible, unstructured data.
notes.simple: Choose a storage method that suits the data and the job. A spreadsheet suits simpler tasks; a database suits structured records; a data warehouse suits large-scale analysis; NoSQL suits flexible data that does not fit traditional tables.
examples: A small shop could use a spreadsheet to keep a simple inventory.
A company could use a data warehouse to analyse sales collected from different sources.
steps: Check whether the task is simple or needs complex data management.
Check whether the data is structured in tables or is flexible and unstructured.
Choose the method that fits the task: spreadsheet, database, data warehouse, or NoSQL.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the four data storage technologies covered in this section.
notes.checkAnswer: Spreadsheets, databases, data warehouses, and NoSQL.

notes.title: Data Visualization
notes.answer: A line graph.
notes.explanation: Data visualization turns information into charts, graphs, and other pictures. These visuals help us quickly notice patterns and understand what data is telling us. Choose a visualization that suits the type of data.
notes.simple: A chart is a picture of data. It can make a lot of information easier to understand quickly.
examples: A bar chart can compare how many students chose each favourite fruit.
A line graph can show how a measurement changes over time.
steps: Identify what the data represents.
Decide whether the data is nominal, ordinal, discrete, or continuous.
Choose a suitable chart or graph for that data type.
Use the visual to look for patterns, trends, or relationships.
notes.checkQuestion: Which visualization could show how a measurement changes over time?
notes.checkAnswer: A bar chart or pie chart is suitable for nominal data because nominal data consists of categories without a specific order.

notes.title: Preparing and Analysing Data
notes.answer: Thematic analysis.
notes.explanation: Data pre-processing gets data ready for analysis by checking its quality, finding problems, and cleaning or organizing it. Analysis then uses suitable methods to find useful information. Numerical data can be studied using measures such as the mean, median, mode, range, variance, and standard deviation. Non-numeric data can be studied using content analysis or thematic analysis.
notes.simple: First check and tidy the data. Then choose a suitable way to study it: use number methods for numeric data and look for words or themes in non-numeric data.
examples: If a score is recorded as 105 when the maximum is 100, it is an error that should be checked and corrected or removed.
For the scores 70, 80, 90, 100, and 110, the mean is 90.
steps: Check whether the data is accurate, complete, reliable, consistent, and up-to-date.
Identify errors, outliers, and possible biases.
Validate completeness and accuracy, then clean the data as needed.
Use quantitative methods for numbers and qualitative methods for non-numeric data.
Interpret the results to discover useful information and draw conclusions.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of analysis could help identify common themes in student essays?
notes.checkAnswer: Quantitative analysis deals with numbers and measurable data; qualitative analysis deals with non-numeric data such as text, images, and sounds.

notes.title: Cloud Storage and Working Together
notes.answer: A backup can help you recover a file if it is accidentally deleted or your computer fails.
notes.explanation: Cloud storage lets you save files online and access them from different devices. Remote access means using a computer, network, or its resources from a distant location. Backups are separate copies that help you recover files if the originals are lost. Collaborative authoring lets several people work on the same document or project together.
notes.simple: Think of cloud storage as an online place for your files. You can reach your files from another device, keep backup copies, and work with other people on shared documents.
examples: Save a school project to Google Drive at home, then open and edit it at school.
Keep a copy of a computer file on Google Drive or a USB so you can recover it if the computer crashes.
steps: Save your file online or make a separate backup copy.
Log in to your cloud account from the device you want to use.
Open the file and continue working.
For a shared project, let group members contribute and edit.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one reason to make a backup of an important file?
notes.checkAnswer: Remote access lets you connect to and use a computer or network from a distant location.

notes.title: How data science turns data into insights
notes.answer: Data science combines computer skills, math, and business knowledge to turn raw data into useful insights.
notes.explanation: Data science uses data to understand problems and make better decisions. It brings together computer science, mathematics and statistics, and business knowledge. A data science workflow moves from identifying a problem to collecting, cleaning, analysing, interpreting, and visualizing data.
notes.simple: Data science is detective work with data: find information, check it, look for clues, understand what they mean, and show the results clearly.
examples: A school collects students’ arrival times, checks the data for errors, looks for patterns, works out likely reasons for lateness, and presents the results in a chart.
A sports team analyses performance data to find patterns and develop better strategies.
steps: Identify and clearly define the problem.
Collect information from suitable sources.
Clean the data by fixing errors and organizing it.
Analyse the data to look for patterns or answers.
Interpret the results and draw conclusions.
Visualize the data with charts or graphs to make it easier to understand.
notes.checkQuestion: In the workflow, what step comes after data collection?
notes.checkAnswer: Data cleaning

notes.title: Big Data and its applications
notes.answer: Big Data is extremely large and complex data that cannot be managed with traditional tools. Its Three Vs are Volume, Velocity, and Variety.
notes.explanation: Big Data is extremely large and complex data that traditional tools cannot manage easily. Its Three Vs describe how much data there is, how quickly it moves, and the different forms it takes.
notes.simple: Think of Big Data as a huge, fast-moving collection of many kinds of information. Special tools help people find useful patterns in it.
examples: Social media posts, likes, and comments shared every day show Big Data's Volume.
A bank analysing transactions to spot unusual activity is an example of a Big Data application.
steps: Identify what is being described: amount, speed, or type of data.
Match it to Volume, Velocity, or Variety.
For an application, state the field and what it uses the data to do.
notes.checkQuestion: Which of the Three Vs means the speed at which data is generated and processed?
notes.checkAnswer: Velocity is the speed at which data is generated and processed.

notes.title: Gathering and understanding data
notes.answer: Data are raw facts gathered about things.
notes.explanation: Data are raw facts gathered about things. We can classify data as qualitative or quantitative, collect it using methods such as surveys, organise it in tables and charts, and use visualizations to understand it. Good data gathering starts by understanding the problem.
notes.simple: Data are facts. Sort and display them clearly so you can understand them and answer questions.
examples: Favourite ice cream flavour is qualitative data; number of students is quantitative, discrete data.
Students' heights are continuous data because they can take measured values within a range.
steps: Understand the problem and decide what information is needed.
Choose a suitable method, such as a survey, to collect the data.
Organise the information in tables or charts.
Analyse and display the data to find patterns and communicate results.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of data is the number of students in a class, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: The number of students is discrete data because it is countable and takes separate whole-number values.

notes.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
notes.answer: Artificial Intelligence denotes the simulation of human thinking ability in computer systems to think and learn in a manner like humans.
notes.explanation: AI is a field of computer science that enables computer systems to simulate human thinking and learning. Its uses include healthcare, education, gaming, transportation, and farming.
notes.simple: AI helps computers do tasks that seem to need human thinking, such as understanding a question or recognizing a picture.
steps: Remember the textbook definition of AI.
Recall the main historical milestones, from the Dartmouth Conference in 1956 to ChatGPT in 2023.
Connect each AI subfield to what it does: learning, language, images, or robots.
Give a real application when asked how AI is used.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two subfields of AI.
notes.checkAnswer: Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and robotics.

notes.title: Explainable and Unexplainable AI Algorithms
notes.answer: Explainable (whitebox) algorithms have a transparent and understandable decision-making process.
notes.explanation: AI algorithms can be grouped by how easy it is to understand their decisions. Whitebox algorithms show an understandable decision-making process; blackbox algorithms make decisions that are not easily interpreted.
notes.simple: Whitebox means you can follow how the AI reached its decision. Blackbox means that process is hard to understand.
examples: A decision tree asks questions such as “Has feathers?” and follows the answers to identify an animal.
A neural network can process an image and identify it as a cat, even though its decision-making process may be difficult to interpret.
steps: Identify whether the decision-making process is transparent and understandable.
If it is, classify the algorithm as explainable (whitebox).
If it is not easily interpreted, classify it as unexplainable (blackbox).
Use examples to support your answer: decision trees are whitebox; neural networks and deep learning models are blackbox examples.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of AI algorithm has a transparent and understandable decision-making process?
notes.checkAnswer: Decision Trees are explainable (whitebox) algorithms.

notes.title: Introduction to Internet of Things (IoT)
notes.answer: IoT is a network of physical objects, or "things," that are equipped with sensors, software, and other technologies to facilitate the exchange of data with other devices and systems over the internet.
notes.explanation: IoT connects physical objects to the internet so they can collect, share, and use data. An IoT system uses sensors, actuators, devices, networks, and data analysis. These parts support applications such as smart homes, healthcare, and transportation. Secure passwords, regular updates, and encryption help protect IoT devices and data.
notes.simple: IoT means everyday objects connect to the internet and share data. Sensors gather information, and connected devices can use it to perform tasks.
examples: In a smart home, connected temperature controls, lights, and surveillance cameras can work as part of an IoT system.
In healthcare, IoT devices can track vital signs and alert healthcare providers in an emergency.
steps: Sensors collect data from the environment.
Networks connect sensors and devices to the internet so they can share data.
Data analysis processes the collected data to gain insights and make decisions.
Devices use the data to perform specific tasks; actuators can act on data to generate output.
Use strong, unique passwords, regular updates, and encryption to improve security.
notes.checkQuestion: Which IoT component detects and measures physical properties such as temperature?
notes.checkAnswer: Sensors collect data from the environment.

notes.title: Benefits, risks, and responsible use of AI and IoT
notes.answer: AI and IoT bring benefits to daily life, work environments, and society, but they also raise concerns such as data privacy and algorithmic bias. Appropriate laws, ethical guidelines, bias-mitigation standards, and security standards help address these concerns.
notes.explanation: AI and IoT can make life, work, and public services more efficient, but they also create risks. Data privacy and algorithmic bias are two key concerns. Laws, ethical guidelines, bias-mitigation standards, and security standards can help address them.
notes.simple: New technology can be helpful, but we must protect people's information and make sure AI treats people fairly.
examples: A smart home device may collect personal information, so it needs strong security to protect that data.
If an AI system learns from biased training data, it may make unfair decisions.
steps: Identify the benefit or risk being discussed.
Explain how it affects people, workplaces, or society.
Give a relevant example.
For a risk, describe a suitable measure to reduce it.
notes.checkQuestion: What can algorithmic bias cause?
notes.checkAnswer: Algorithmic bias can lead to unfair outcomes.

notes.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things
notes.answer: AI and IoT are technologies that can make services more useful and connected, but they should be developed and used ethically.
notes.explanation: AI enables computers to perform tasks that usually require human intelligence, while IoT connects physical devices so they can collect and exchange data. Both technologies can improve services and daily life, but they also raise concerns about privacy, security, fairness, jobs and accountability.
notes.simple: AI helps computers do intelligent tasks. IoT lets connected devices share information. Both can be useful, but people must use them responsibly.
steps: AI means machines can perform tasks that normally need human intelligence.
Machine learning uses data so a system can learn patterns and make predictions.
A whitebox model has decisions that people can understand; a blackbox model is difficult to interpret.
IoT devices use sensors, connectivity and data processing to share information and provide services.
Check AI and IoT systems for security, privacy, fairness and effects on people’s work.
notes.checkQuestion: What does IoT connect?
notes.checkAnswer: IoT connects devices that collect and exchange data.

notes.title: Choosing and using computer technology responsibly
notes.answer: Responsible computer usage includes protecting personal information, making wise choices about hardware and software, and behaving respectfully and ethically online.
notes.explanation: Responsible computer usage means choosing suitable, secure hardware and software and using technology thoughtfully. Check that your equipment is safe, efficient for your tasks, and compatible with the programs you need.
notes.simple: Choose computer parts and programs that are safe, suit your task, and work well together.
examples: A computer without updated antivirus software may be more at risk from viruses or hackers.
An old computer may run a new video game slowly or may not run it at all.
steps: Identify what you need the computer to do.
Choose hardware and software suitable for that task.
Check the software's system requirements against your computer's specifications.
Use updated, secure software to help protect your information.
notes.checkQuestion: What should you compare to check whether software will work on your computer?
notes.checkAnswer: Check the software's system requirements and compare them with your computer's specifications.

notes.title: Using Digital Platforms Safely and Securely
notes.answer: Use a strong, unique password and enable 2FA.
notes.explanation: Safe operation means using digital platforms and devices in a way that protects you from harm and avoids unwanted issues. For example, use strong, unique passwords and avoid unknown links. Secure use adds protections such as two-factor authentication (2FA), avoiding public Wi-Fi for sensitive transactions, checking account activity, and backing up important data.
notes.simple: Keep your accounts and information protected: use good passwords, be careful online, and keep a backup of important data.
examples: A message asks for your password through an unfamiliar link. Do not click it; check who sent it and verify the request another way.
You need to check your bank account. Wait until you can use a secure, private network rather than public Wi-Fi.
steps: Create a strong, unique password for each account.
Turn on Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) where it is available.
Do not click unknown links or download files from untrusted sources.
Avoid sensitive transactions on public Wi-Fi.
Check privacy settings and account activity regularly.
Back up important data to an external drive or a cloud storage service.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two ways to protect an online account.
notes.checkAnswer: Use a strong, unique password and enable 2FA.

notes.title: Best Practices in Online Behavior
notes.answer: Use online services responsibly: protect personal information, use strong passwords, and review privacy settings.
notes.explanation: Use digital platforms carefully: think before posting, be cautious with unknown emails, protect cloud accounts with strong passwords, and download apps only from trusted sources. Review privacy settings so you control who can see your information.
notes.simple: Think before sharing, keep your accounts protected, and use trusted apps and services.
examples: Do not post your home address publicly on social media.
Download apps only from trusted sources such as Google Play Store or Apple App Store.
steps: Think before posting and keep private details out of public posts.
Be careful with emails from unknown senders; do not open harmful links or attachments.
Use strong passwords to protect cloud and other online accounts.
Download apps only from trusted sources.
Review privacy settings regularly and update them to protect your information.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one way to protect your information on a digital platform.
notes.checkAnswer: Use strong, unique passwords and review privacy settings regularly.

notes.title: Legal and Ethical Frameworks
notes.answer: Privacy laws are rules set by the government to protect our personal information. Data ethics guides the fair and responsible collection, storage, and use of information.
notes.explanation: Privacy laws set rules for how organisations handle personal information. They help protect it from misuse and unauthorized access. Data ethics guides people to collect, store, and use information fairly. Important principles include transparency, respect for privacy, consent, data minimization, security, and accountability.
notes.simple: Privacy laws help keep your personal information safe. Data ethics means treating information and the people it belongs to fairly.
steps: Ask for consent before collecting someone's data.
Collect only the data that is needed.
Keep the data secure from unauthorized access.
Use and share the data responsibly.
Take responsibility and act if something goes wrong.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two principles of data ethics.
notes.checkAnswer: Privacy laws are government rules that protect personal information; data ethics means handling information fairly and responsibly.

notes.title: Intellectual Property Rights
notes.answer: A trademark protects a company’s logo.
notes.explanation: Intellectual property rights protect creations and ideas. Copyright protects original works, trademarks distinguish a company’s products or services, and patents protect new inventions or processes. Using or sharing protected work without permission can be unethical and illegal. Software piracy is the illegal copying, distribution, or use of software.
notes.simple: Creators have rights over what they create. Do not copy or use their work without permission.
examples: An author’s book is protected by copyright.
A company’s logo is a trademark; a new invention may be protected by a patent.
steps: Identify what is being protected: an original work, a brand symbol or name, or an invention.
Match it to copyright, trademark, or patent.
Use or share someone else’s protected work only with permission or a valid licence.
notes.checkQuestion: Which intellectual property right protects a company’s logo?
notes.checkAnswer: Copyright protects original works, trademarks identify products or services, and patents protect new inventions or processes.

notes.title: Responsible Internet Use
notes.answer: Use the internet safely and respectfully, protect your privacy, check information, and maintain a healthy balance between online and offline activities.
notes.explanation: Responsible internet use means staying safe, checking information, protecting privacy, treating others respectfully, and balancing online time with offline life.
notes.simple: Use the internet carefully: check what you read, protect your personal information, be kind to people, and take breaks.
examples: Before trusting a health claim online, compare it with information from several trustworthy websites.
If someone sends you a suspicious link, do not click it; use the platform’s report or block tools if needed.
steps: Check important information against several trustworthy sources.
Avoid sensational headlines and suspicious links.
Use private browsing and do not enter personal information on unfamiliar websites.
Set time limits, take breaks, and include offline activities.
Set social media privacy controls and interact respectfully.
Report and block cyberbullying, and support the person being bullied.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one way to check online information and one way to protect your privacy during research.
notes.checkAnswer: Check several trustworthy sources and avoid sharing personal information on unfamiliar websites.

notes.title: How Computing Affects Society
notes.answer: Computing has benefits, such as instant communication, and risks, such as misinformation. Check information using reliable sources before sharing it.
notes.explanation: Computing affects how people work, communicate, trade, and share culture. It brings benefits such as easier communication and new jobs, but it can also create problems such as cyberbullying, misinformation, and reduced privacy. Use technology thoughtfully: check information before sharing it, respect other people’s work, and balance security with ease of use.
notes.simple: Computers make many things easier, but people need to use them carefully so the benefits do not cause harm.
examples: A video call lets people communicate across long distances.
A false health story shared on social media can mislead people.
steps: Identify the area affected, such as communication, trade, culture, jobs, or privacy.
State one benefit or change computing brings to that area.
Mention a related risk or trade-off if the question asks for one.
Give a clear example and explain its effect.
notes.checkQuestion: What should you do before believing or sharing a story you see on social media?
notes.checkAnswer: Verify information with reliable sources before believing or sharing it.

notes.title: Responsible Computer Usage
notes.answer: Use computers safely and responsibly by protecting your data, making careful choices, respecting privacy and intellectual property, and checking information before relying on it.
notes.explanation: Use computers thoughtfully: protect your information, choose compatible hardware and software, respect other people’s rights, and check that online information is reliable.
notes.simple: Stay safe online, respect other people’s work and privacy, and think carefully before you click or share.
examples: Use a strong, unique password and enable two-factor authentication.
Check who can see your social media posts before sharing them.
steps: Choose hardware and software that fit your needs and work together.
Keep devices and software updated, and use antivirus software.
Protect accounts with strong, unique passwords and 2FA.
Avoid suspicious links, downloads, messages, and sensitive transactions on public Wi-Fi.
Use privacy settings and share personal information carefully.
Respect intellectual property and check online sources before trusting them.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two ways to help keep an online account secure.
notes.checkAnswer: Use strong, unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication.

notes.title: Entrepreneurship and why it matters
notes.answer: Entrepreneurship is the process of starting a new business or organization. It can create jobs, support economic growth, and encourage innovation.
notes.explanation: An entrepreneur starts and runs a new business or organization. Entrepreneurs identify a need, develop an idea, and take a risk to make it real. Their businesses can create jobs, support economic growth, and bring new ideas and products.
notes.simple: An entrepreneur spots a need, thinks of a way to meet it, and starts a business—even though it might not succeed.
examples: A neighborhood bakery started to serve its community is a local example of entrepreneurship.
Facebook, Google, and Apple began as small tech companies founded by entrepreneurs with innovative ideas.
steps: Spot a need in the market.
Think of a product, process, or service that could meet that need.
Take the risk of starting a business or organization.
Run the business and create value for customers.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the origin and meaning of the word entrepreneur?
notes.checkAnswer: The word entrepreneur comes from a French word meaning “to undertake.” Entrepreneurs undertake the task of starting and running new businesses.

notes.title: Entrepreneurship in the Digital Landscape
notes.answer: Digital entrepreneurship uses internet-based tools and technologies to create and run businesses.
notes.explanation: Digital technologies help entrepreneurs operate businesses, connect with customers and sell products online. Tools such as social media, mobile apps, cloud computing, big data analytics and e-commerce platforms can help a business reach more people and work efficiently.
notes.simple: Digital entrepreneurship means using internet-based tools and services to start or run a business.
examples: A small clothing business can use Instagram to show products and answer customers’ questions.
A Pakistani business can use an e-commerce platform to list products, manage orders and sell to customers in different cities.
steps: Choose a product or service to sell.
Use digital channels to promote it and connect with customers.
Use an e-commerce platform to display products and manage online sales.
Use customer and sales information to make better business decisions.
notes.checkQuestion: What does an e-commerce platform help a business do?
notes.checkAnswer: An e-commerce platform lets a business sell goods online and can help it manage inventory, payments and customer service.

notes.title: Digital Tools and Platforms
notes.answer: Digital tools and platforms help businesses research markets, promote products, and sell online.
notes.explanation: Digital tools help people do tasks efficiently. For example, Google Docs lets users create and edit documents online and collaborate in real time. Market research tools help businesses learn about customers and competitors; online marketing tools help promote products; e-commerce platforms help sell products and manage payments and customer support.
notes.simple: These are online helpers for running a business: some help you learn about customers, some help you promote your business, and some help you sell online.
examples: Google Analytics tracks website traffic and user behavior.
Shopify helps a business create and manage an online store.
steps: Use market research tools to understand customers, competitors, and market trends.
Use online marketing tools to promote products through digital channels.
Use e-commerce platforms to set up online stores, manage payments, and support customers.
notes.checkQuestion: Which tool can conduct online surveys to gather customer feedback?
notes.checkAnswer: SurveyMonkey conducts online surveys to gather customer feedback.

notes.title: Finding a business idea
notes.answer: Identify what people need or want, then develop and test a solution using design thinking.
notes.explanation: Business ideas often begin by noticing what people need or want. Surveys, market research and observation help identify these needs. Design thinking then gives a five-step way to develop and test a solution.
notes.simple: Find out what people need, then use a creative process to make and test a solution.
examples: Observing that online shopping is popular in Pakistan can lead to ideas for e-commerce platforms suited to local preferences.
Students could develop an app that gives farmers in rural Pakistan weather forecasts and market prices.
steps: Identify a need or problem people have.
Use surveys and questionnaires, market research, or observation to understand it.
Use design thinking: empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test.
Gather feedback and improve the solution.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the first step in design thinking?
notes.checkAnswer: Empathizing.

notes.title: Developing a Business Plan
notes.answer: A business plan sets out business goals and strategies, market analysis, a revenue model, and digital marketing strategies.
notes.explanation: A business plan is a detailed document that outlines your business goals and the strategies you will use to achieve them. It helps an entrepreneur understand customers and competitors, plan how the business will earn money, and decide how to promote and improve its product or service.
notes.simple: A business plan is a roadmap. It explains what a business wants to do and how it will do it.
examples: An online bookstore could research what students read, sell books through an online page, and promote special offers on social media.
A business could make a simple prototype of a product, collect customer feedback, and improve it.
steps: Set out the business goals and strategies.
Research the target market, customers, and competitors.
Plan how the business will earn income.
Choose online ways to promote the business.
Make a prototype and improve the idea using feedback.
notes.checkQuestion: What are two things an entrepreneur should include in a business plan?
notes.checkAnswer: Research customers and competitors, decide how the business will earn money, and plan how to promote it.

notes.title: Planning a Digital Business
notes.answer: A business plan describes the market, customers, business strategies and ways the business will earn revenue.
notes.explanation: Entrepreneurship means starting a business or organisation and developing ideas into useful products or services. Digital tools help entrepreneurs understand customers, promote products and sell to people online. A business plan explains how a business will operate and earn income.
notes.simple: Find a real need, plan a useful solution, and use suitable tools to reach customers.
examples: A student can use an online survey to find out which books local students need, then sell those books through an online bookstore.
A farmer-focused business could use design thinking to learn farmers’ problems and test a simple service before launching it.
steps: Identify a customer need using research, surveys or observation.
Develop a useful idea and improve it by understanding the users.
Plan the market, income, costs and strategies in a business plan.
Use digital tools to promote and sell the product or service.
Consider how the business can support social, environmental and economic sustainability.
notes.checkQuestion: What does market analysis help a business understand?
notes.checkAnswer: Market analysis is the study of customers, their needs and competitors.

quiz.stem: What is the primary function of a system?

quiz.stem: What is one of the fundamental concepts of any system?

An objective is fundamental because it describes what the system is intended to achieve.
A system’s age does not define its fundamental nature.
A system’s price is not a fundamental concept of systems.

quiz.stem: What is an example of a simple system?
rationales: The human body is a complex system with many interacting parts.
A computer network is generally more complex than a simple system.
A thermostat regulating temperature is a simple system that senses temperature and controls heating or cooling.

quiz.stem: What type of environment remains unchanged unless the system provides an output?
rationales: A dynamic environment changes over time, whether or not the system produces an output.
A static environment remains unchanged unless an output from the system affects it.
A deterministic system produces predictable results from given inputs; this does not describe an unchanged environment.
A non-deterministic system may produce unpredictable results; this does not describe an unchanged environment.

quiz.stem: What are the basic components of a system?
rationales: Users, hardware, and software can be parts of some systems but do not describe the basic components of a system in general.

Inputs, outputs, and processes describe a common way of representing system operations, but not the full set of basic components asked for here.
Sensors, actuators, and controllers are components of some control systems, not systems in general.

quiz.stem: What concept does the theory of systems aim to understand?

quiz.stem: What role does the Operating System (OS) play in a computer?

quiz.stem: Which of the following describes the Von Neumann architecture's main characteristic?

Single memory store for both program instructions and data

Parallel instruction execution is not the defining characteristic of Von Neumann architecture.
Von Neumann architecture uses a single memory store for both program instructions and data.
Using multiple CPUs is not the defining characteristic of Von Neumann architecture.

quiz.stem: What is a disadvantage of the Von Neumann architecture?
options: Complex design due to separate memory spaces
Difficult to modify programs stored in memory
Bottleneck due to single memory space for instructions and data
Lack of flexibility in executing instructions
rationales: Separate memory spaces are not a design feature of the Von Neumann architecture.
Programs stored in memory can generally be modified, so this is not its key disadvantage.
Sharing a single memory and communication path for instructions and data can create a bottleneck.
Von Neumann architecture is flexible in executing instructions; its key disadvantage is the shared-memory bottleneck.

quiz.stem: Which of the following transports data inside a computer among different components?

The System Bus transports data among a computer’s components.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a system?

An organized set of components working together to perform a function

A system may have several components and an environment.

quiz.stem: In system theory, what does a system objective describe?

Size does not state what the system is meant to achieve.

quiz.stem: Why is communication among components important in a system?

An environment with no external factors

quiz.stem: A car is an example of which kind of system, according to the section's examples?

quiz.stem: Which environment remains unchanged while the system works internally, unless the system provides an output?

quiz.stem: Which description matches a deterministic system, as defined in the section?
